pages.title: Fractions can describe an average, not a fractional electron

blocks.text: Charge-balance arithmetic sometimes gives an oxidation number such as +8/3. Does that mean an atom loses a fraction of one electron? No. The result can be an average over atoms in different environments or oxidation states.
In Fe₃O₄, oxygen totals −8, so the three Fe total +8 and average +8/3. Its mixed Fe(II)/Fe(III) description contains one Fe at +2 and two at +3 per formula unit.

pages.transition: A structural example makes the average clearer.

pages.title: Use structure to interpret formal averages

blocks.text: In C₃O₂, the structure O=C=C=C=O assigns each terminal C +2 from its C=O bond, while the central C is 0. The average is (2 + 0 + 2)/3 = +4/3. Carbon–carbon bonds do not change the assignment between identical atoms.

In S₄O₆²⁻, total S oxidation number is +10, averaging +2.5. Structural analysis assigns +5 to each terminal sulfur and 0 to the two inner sulfurs. The molecular formula alone supplies only the average.
Oxidation states are bookkeeping assignments; a structural formula can distinguish atoms that the empirical composition groups together.

pages.transition: Balancing uses the total electron changes rather than assuming every average is an individual charge.

pages.title: Balance changes before water and charge

blocks.text: The oxidation-number method matches total oxidation-number increases to total decreases, then completes atom and charge balance for the stated medium. Start with correct species formulas; never change subscripts to force a balance.
In Cr₂O₇²⁻ + SO₃²⁻ → Cr³⁺ + SO₄²⁻, each Cr changes +6 → +3, so two Cr gain six electrons in total. Each S changes +4 → +6 and loses two. Therefore three sulfite ions match one dichromate ion.

pages.transition: Complete the acidic-medium equation and verify every atom.

pages.title: Worked oxidation-number balance in acid

blocks.text: Start Cr₂O₇²⁻ + 3SO₃²⁻ → 2Cr³⁺ + 3SO₄²⁻. Left O = 7 + 9 = 16; right O = 12, so add 4H₂O on the right. This requires 8H⁺ on the left. Final: Cr₂O₇²⁻ + 3SO₃²⁻ + 8H⁺ → 2Cr³⁺ + 3SO₄²⁻ + 4H₂O.
Charge left is −2 − 6 + 8 = 0; charge right is +6 − 6 = 0. Cr, S, O and H also match. The medium supplies H⁺ and water without changing the specified redox species.

pages.transition: The half-reaction method separates the same electron accounting explicitly.

pages.title: Balance each half-reaction systematically

blocks.text: In acidic medium, balance atoms other than O and H first. Add H₂O to balance O, H⁺ to balance H, then electrons to balance charge. Multiply the halves so their electron counts agree, add, and cancel identical species.
Balancing atoms alone is insufficient for an ionic reaction. Electrons are inserted on the side needed to make the half-reaction charges equal, then disappear from the overall equation.

pages.transition: Apply the method to dichromate oxidising iron(II).

pages.title: Worked acidic half-reactions

blocks.text: Oxidation: Fe²⁺ → Fe³⁺ + e⁻. Reduction skeleton: Cr₂O₇²⁻ → 2Cr³⁺. Balance O with 7H₂O on the right and H with 14H⁺ on the left. Charge left is +12 and right +6, so add 6e⁻ on the left: Cr₂O₇²⁻ + 14H⁺ + 6e⁻ → 2Cr³⁺ + 7H₂O.
Each dichromate accepts six electrons, while one Fe²⁺ supplies only one. Multiply the iron half by six before adding; adding unscaled halves would violate electron conservation.

pages.transition: Add the matched halves and check the complete equation.

pages.title: The combined iron–dichromate equation

blocks.text: Cr₂O₇²⁻ + 14H⁺ + 6Fe²⁺ → 2Cr³⁺ + 7H₂O + 6Fe³⁺. The six electrons cancel. Total charge left is −2 + 14 + 12 = +24; right is +6 + 18 = +24.
The coefficient ratio is 1 mol dichromate to 6 mol Fe²⁺. For 0.0100 mol dichromate, the equivalent Fe²⁺ amount is 6 × 0.0100 = 0.0600 mol, assuming the stated acidic reaction proceeds completely.

pages.transition: Basic solutions require removing the H⁺ introduced during balancing.

pages.title: Convert a balanced half-reaction to basic medium

blocks.text: A reliable procedure first balances as though acidic, then adds enough OH⁻ to both sides to neutralise every H⁺. Replace H⁺ + OH⁻ by H₂O and cancel water appearing on both sides. The final basic equation should contain no leftover H⁺.
Permanganate reduction to MnO₂ in base is MnO₄⁻ + 2H₂O + 3e⁻ → MnO₂ + 4OH⁻. Check: O = 6 on both sides, H = 4, and charge = −4.

pages.transition: Combine it with an oxidation half to finish a basic-medium example.

pages.title: Worked basic balance with bromide

blocks.text: Oxidation in base: Br⁻ + 6OH⁻ → BrO₃⁻ + 3H₂O + 6e⁻. Multiply the preceding Mn reduction by two, then add. Cancel 6e⁻, 3H₂O and 6OH⁻ where appropriate. Final: 2MnO₄⁻ + Br⁻ + H₂O → 2MnO₂ + BrO₃⁻ + 2OH⁻.
Charge is −3 on both sides; Mn = 2, Br = 1, O = 9 and H = 2. Mn gains six electrons in total while Br loses six. The explicit medium determines whether manganese appears as Mn²⁺ or MnO₂.

pages.transition: Revise the structural-average and balancing checks before attempting new equations.

pages.title: Revision: conserve atoms and charge together

blocks.text: Fractional oxidation numbers may be averages; use structure to distinguish individual atoms. In balancing, match total oxidation increase and reduction decrease, not just per-atom changes.

Acidic half-reaction steps: other atoms → O with H₂O → H with H⁺ → charge with e⁻. For base, neutralise H⁺ using OH⁻ on both sides and cancel water. Verify every element, total charge, electron cancellation and the specified medium.

questions.question: Why is +8/3 for Fe in Fe₃O₄ not a fractional ionic charge?
questions.answer: It is the average for one Fe(II) and two Fe(III) contributions per formula unit.

questions.question: How many electrons does one Cr₂O₇²⁻ gain on becoming 2Cr³⁺?
questions.answer: Each Cr gains three, so two Cr gain six in total.

questions.question: Why does one dichromate need three sulfite ions in the stated reaction?
questions.answer: Dichromate gains six electrons, while each S(+4) → S(+6) loses two, requiring three sulfites.

questions.question: What extra check is needed beyond atoms for an ionic equation?
questions.answer: Total electrical charge must also be equal on both sides.

questions.question: How are acidic balancing H⁺ ions removed for a basic equation?
questions.answer: Add the same number of OH⁻ to both sides, form water from H⁺ + OH⁻, then cancel redundant water.

questions.question: Can the same permanganate half-reaction be used for every medium?
questions.answer: No. Products depend on the reaction conditions; the stated acidic or basic product must be used.
